title: Socket controllers
summary: SocketRoute marks a controller class that keeps a WebSocket open, as Jakarta's @ServerEndpoint does. Tachyon makes one object of the class for each connection, so its fields hold that connection's state. OnOpen, OnMessage, OnClose and OnError mark the methods that run when a browser connects, sends a message, leaves, or when a method fails. Each message is JSON text, and Tachyon checks it against the model type of the OnMessage parameter first. The session sends messages back, and openSessions() (open_sessions() in Python, Ruby, Lua and Rust, OpenSessions() in Go, C# and F#, getOpenSessions() in Java) returns every open connection of the same path, so one message can go to every tab. In Go, session.Request() returns the request that opened the socket as an *http.Request, with the query string and the headers. When OnOpen or OnMessage fails, OnError runs and the socket stays open, as in Jakarta. In the browser, SocketRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the messages and publishes each one as its model's event, and the client's send(message) writes to the socket. The SocketRequest client is JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Ruby, Rust, Dart, Swift, Kotlin, C#, Lua, Python, F# or C++ (a Dart client is a method of an abstract interface class such as `void receive(ChatMessage message);`, held by the page for the Dart service that keeps it in a `@Needs` field, and gets `Future<void> send(Object? message)`, which fails with a code such as `HTTP_NETWORK`; a Rust client is a trait method such as `fn receive(&self, message: ChatMessage)`, held by the page for the Rust service that keeps it in a `#[Needs]` field, and gets `send(message).await`). A Go client is an interface method such as `Receive(message ChatMessage)`; the page holds the socket for the Go service that keeps the client in a `// @Needs` field, the service receives each message with `// @OnEvent`, and the generated `Send(message any) error` writes to the socket and returns an error code such as `HTTP_NETWORK` instead of a rejected promise. A Swift client is a protocol method held the same way, and its generated `send(_ message:) async throws` throws those codes. A Kotlin client is an interface method such as `fun receive(message: ChatMessage)`; the page holds the socket for the Kotlin web service that keeps the client in a `@Needs` field, and the generated `suspend fun send(message: Any)` waits for the page and throws an error whose message starts with the code, such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. A C# client is an interface method such as `void Receive(Models.ChatMessage message);` in a browser C# service that keeps it in a `[Needs]` field; the service receives each message with `[OnEvent]`, and the generated `Task Send(object message)` throws a `BehaviorError` with a code such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. A Lua client is an empty method such as `function ChatClient:receive(message)` in a Lua service that keeps it in a typed `-- @Needs` field; the service receives each message with `-- @OnEvent`, and the generated `client:send(message)` raises a `BehaviorError` with a code such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. A Python client is a `Protocol` method such as `def receive(self, message: ChatMessage) -> None: ...`, held the same way for the Python service that keeps it in a `Needs` field, and the generated `async def send(self, message)` raises a `BehaviorError` with a code such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. An F# client is an abstract member such as `abstract Receive: ChatMessage -> unit` in a browser F# service that keeps it in a `[<Needs>]` property; the service receives each message with `[<OnEvent>]`, and the generated `Send(message: obj) : Task` raises a `BehaviorError` with the same codes. A C++ client is a method of an `[[HTTPClient]]` class such as `[[SocketRequest]] void receive(const ChatMessage& message);`, held the same way for the C++ service that keeps it in a `[[Needs]]` field, and the generated `Task<void> send(message)` throws a `tachyon::http::HttpRequestException` with a code such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. Java refuses SocketRequest with TY1308, and its services receive the messages with OnEvent. Sockets are written in any Yon language. Tachyon guards every socket (ADR 0060): a message is JSON text of at most 64 KiB; a message that is not JSON or does not fit the model closes the socket with code 1007, a binary message with 1003, and a larger message with 1009. Five minutes without a message closes it with 1001, a socket lasts at most one hour, and a page from another origin gets 403. `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class says who may connect; Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before it opens the socket.
